en: Preface to the Commentary on the *Mūlamadhyamaka-kārikā*, composed by Jizang.
Sengrui was a native of Qu-le in Chang-le during the Wei dynasty. He entered the monastic order in his youth and relied upon Dharma Master Sengxian.
As a disciple,
he once attended lectures by Zhongshan Kangsenglang and frequently raised criticisms and challenges;
his master highly praised and commended him for this.
At the age of twenty-four, he traveled extensively through famous regions,
constantly propagating and lecturing on the teachings.
He was upright, simple, noble, and pure.
One source states:
"Fangjian’s lofty character was as firm as ice and frost.
When Kumārajīva arrived in Chang’an, he followed him to study under his guidance."
Of the three thousand disciples, only eight entered the inner sanctum;
Hui was their leader.
The text says:
When old, he was Rongrui;
when young, he was Daosheng and Sengzhao.
Kumārajīva sighed and said:
"The transmission of my teachings is entrusted to Dao Rong, Tan Ying, and Seng Rui.
After Kumārajīva finished translating the *Satyasiddhi-śāstra*, he commanded Seng Rui to lecture on it and said to Dao Rong:
In this polemical treatise, there are seven points where the Abhidharma is refuted;
these are somewhat obscure in their expression.
If you can identify them without asking me, you may truly be called a man of extraordinary talent.
Rong said,
"That person possesses a certain degree of intellectual power and need not necessarily have received formal instruction;
he has analyzed [the matter] exhaustively, leaving nothing behind."
The multitude marveled at and revered him all the more.
When Emperor Yao Xing heard of Daoxuan’s exemplary conduct,
he asked Yao Song, the Marquis of Ancheng:
"Who is this person Rui?
Song said,
"He is the pine and cypress of the state of Wei."
Later, he personally brought Zong睿 (Zongrui) to see him,
saying to Song:
"This is truly a model for all under heaven."
How could it be that he merely protected through his deeds?
Thereupon, his excellent reputation spread far and wide, reaching both distant and near lands.

He composed prefaces for the *Madhyamaka-śāstra*, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra*, the *Dhyāna-sūtra*, and others, which have been transmitted to the world as elegant compositions.
He was sixty-one years old.
He composed the *Preface to the Zhonglun* (Treatise on the Middle), for which there were not merely one author;
Tanyi also composed the *Preface to the Yishu* (Commentary on the Meaning).
Daolang of Hexi also composed a preface to the treatise;
however, the literary style and meaning of Master Rui’s work fully encompass both principle and phenomena, and its reasoning is subtle and profound.
The Venerable of Xinghuang Monastery would regularly read it whenever he gave lectures.
This is indeed one who believes in and loves antiquity, transmitting without creating;
yet, as the text contains subtle obscurities,
I have provided a brief commentary upon it.
This single introduction is divided into seven sections:
first, a general indication of the persons and the Dharma;
second, an explanation of the title.
Third, the prolegomenon on dependent origination;
fourth, the praise and explanation of its efficacy;
fifth, the description of the commentator Qingmu (Candrakīrti).
Sixth is the extensive praise of the four treatises;
seventh is the author’s self-deprecation.
The five hundred verses of the *Madhyamaka-śāstra* indicate the doctrine that has been composed.
The Bodhisattva Nāgārjuna composed this preface concerning the person who was able to create [this work].
The Way does not operate in isolation;
its propagation depends upon individuals.
Therefore, the preceding section clarifies the Way that is propagated,
while the subsequent section introduces the person who propagates the Way.
Furthermore, the title "Treatise on the Five Hundred Verses" emphasizes the importance of the Dharma.
Nāgārjuna Bodhisattva was a person of supreme honor.
Furthermore, the first phrase distinguishes the dharma from the two extremes,
while the latter phrase differentiates those of the Hīnayāna.
Regarding what is called the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā*, its profound meaning has been fully set forth.
Now, having explained the preface, I shall briefly clarify five points.
First, this treatise determines the partiality or correctness of the Buddha’s Dharma.
It adjudicates the root causes of gain and loss;
thus, Nāgārjuna designated this work as the *Madhyamaka-śāstra*.
Second, it is because this text expounds the principle of reality within the Middle Way.
It is called the *Madhyamaka-śāstra* because it is named according to the actual principle it elucidates.
As the "Chapter on Karma" states:
"Because the meaning clarified in this treatise is free from the views of annihilationism and eternalism, it is called the *Madhyamaka-śāstra*."
Third, regarding the works composed by Nāgārjuna, there are generally three treatises:
first, the extensive version, the *Vigrahavyāvartanī*;
second, the intermediate version, the *Śūnyatāsaptati*; and third, the concise version, the *Vaidalyaprakaraṇa*.
This is now a moderate exposition;
therefore, it is discussed in the *Zhonglun* (Treatise on the Middle).
Fourth, the meaning is expressed through the text.
This treatise has no introduction preceding it and concludes with a brief summary of its remaining momentum, consisting only of the main text.
Because it expresses its meaning through the words, it is titled the *Madhyamaka-śāstra* (Treatise on the Middle).
Fifth, the Great Being Nāgārjuna was a practitioner of the Middle Way.
It was composed by one who follows the Middle Way;
it is titled the *Madhyamaka-śāstra* because it is named after its author.
As for the "five hundred verses": [it consists of] five hundred stanzas.
Having previously indicated their titles, we now introduce the number of verses.
There are two kinds of verses:
the first is the *śloka* verse.
This refers to the numerical method of the Hu (Indians) for counting sūtras and dharmas;
it is what is called a "universal verse" (gāthā).
As for the term "universal verse":
Do not inquire whether it is in prose or verse;
provided that the number of characters reaches thirty-two,
it is then a verse.
The second is the distinct verse (gāthā),
which refers to verses formed by concluding lines,
regardless of whether they consist of four, five, six, or seven syllables.
Providing merely that the four lines are complete constitutes a *gāthā*.
As for the term *gāthā*, its full foreign pronunciation should be *geya*;
it is also transliterated as *qíyè* (祇夜).
Now, to show both the comprehensive and the abbreviated versions, they are simply weighed and formed into *gāthās*.
A *gāthā* is a verse; it is a stanza.
Furthermore, as for the term *gāthā*:
This phonetic transcription also exists in the Chinese *Han shu*.
Its gloss explains it as having the meaning of "exhaustion" (*kṣaya*);
that is, because the meaning is clearly and completely exhausted, it is termed a *gāthā*.
However, there are generally two types of verses used for concluding sections:
first, the *lōka-gāthā*,
which refers to verses that summarize the prose (*dīrgha-pada*).
The second is the gāthā-verse,
which refers to the independent verse (udāna).
In this treatise, the term "verse" (gāthā) is used as follows:
Regarding the two categories of "comprehensive" and "distinct," the latter refers to the distinct verses (gāthās).
The final two passages refer to the independent verses (udāna-gāthās).
As for the "five hundred": [text continues].
Examining the text closely, there are in total four hundred and forty-six verses;
this may represent the full grand total,
or perhaps the translation was not exhaustive.
Because it is named after its original source, it is weighed at five hundred [units].
Among the various sutras and treatises, there are three types:
first, those consisting solely of prose (*gadya*).
This refers to the *Śata-śāstra*.
The second [work] consists solely of verses;
such is this text.
The three [categories] possess two kinds [of characteristics].
Regarding works such as the *Dvādaśamukha-śāstra*,
the *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā* by Nāgārjuna states:
Some may delight in prose;
some may delight in verse;
and some may delight in ornate compositions consisting of mixed prose and verse.
What each person cherishes differs;
I follow them and do not abandon them.
This being so regarding the three treatises, it is likewise for the others.
The principles of the sūtras are consistently thus.
As for Nāgārjuna,
according to the Sanskrit pronunciation, he should be called Gaṇavṛddha.
*Kaṇa* means "dragon.
*Pukkhala* means "tree.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
*Tuṅga-ma* means "dragon.
*Phullikṣā* is the general name for a tree;
its specific name is *Añjana*.
Just as with the pear and plum trees here [in this world], one asks:
"What is the spiritual rank of Nāgārjuna?
The answer is: "The traces of the sages are boundless; their high or low status is not easily fathomed."
Relying solely on the sūtras and commentaries to describe its depth and shallowness,
Master Rui stated:
"Its merit matches the Ten Stages, and its model serves as a pattern for the position of the Future Buddha."
This is a person who has exhausted their studies.
Tradition says:
"The sun of wisdom has already set."
This person causes [the truth] to shine once more.
The world has been steeped in darkness for a long time;
this person awakens it and leads it to study.
Foreigners have established temples for him and serve him as they do a Buddha;
how can one know that this was not a Buddha manifesting himself as a bodhisattva?
Master Huiyuan of Mount Kuang said:
His name was Guandong; he possessed the virtues of the stages of the path and was fully endowed with the three types of patience (*kṣānti*).
He was also a noble personage of the tenth stage (*bhūmi*).
According to the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*.
The Bodhisattva Mahāmati asked:
"World-Honored One, after your parinirvāṇa, who will uphold the Buddha-dharma?
The Buddha replied:
"Mahāmati, you should know that in a great kingdom in South India there is a bhikṣu of great virtue named Bodhisattva Nāgārjuna."
He expounds the unsurpassed Dharma of the Mahāyāna for others,
is able to shatter views of existence and non-existence,
and dwells in the first stage, the Stage of Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*).
Regarding the phrase "reborn in the Land of Peaceful Nurturing" (An-yang guo),
there are differing interpretations.
The older tradition states:
Nāgārjuna was a person of the first bhūmi.
Dao’an of Guannei, while studying the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, said:
"This is Nāgārjuna leading sentient beings to enter the first bhūmi."
In reality, he is a person of the tenth stage (*daśabhūmi*).
Question: On what stages does he rely?
Answer: If one says he is on the first stage, then he relies on two stages.
If one is a student of ultimate inquiry, then the fourth reliance is on the person.
Question: What are these four reliances?
Answer: For now, let us provide a single judgment.
In the Hīnayāna, a person possessing afflictions prior to the path of seeing is the first reliance;
a Srotāpanna or Sakṛdāgāmin is the second reliance;
and an Anāgāmin is the third reliance.
The fourth reliance for the Arhats:
according to the Mahāyāna perspective, looking toward the ten stages of dedication (*daśa-pratipatti*), this constitutes the first reliance;
from the first stage (*bhūmi*) up to the seventh stage constitutes the second reliance.
The eighth and ninth stages are the third reliance;
the tenth stage is the fourth reliance.
As in the *Laṅkāvatāra*, this is the second reliance.
Master Rui is the fourth reliance;
for in the Dharma of Śākyamuni Buddha, there is no separate community of bodhisattvas,
and Nāgārjuna was a person who had left the household life.
Therefore, based on the stages of the Hīnayāna,
the term "stages that penetrate the path" (*guandao wei*) is used as a general designation for the bodhisattva stages.
His virtue is complete in the three kinds of patience, which means faith and compliance with non-arising.
Question: Does Nāgārjuna have any other names?
Answer: Yes.
The *Madhyamaka-śāstra-anuvyākhyāna* was composed by Vasubandhu.
Regarding what is called the *Madhyamaka-śāstra-anuvyākhyāna*:
Extensively citing scriptures such as the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, he provides proof and explanation for the "eight negations.
These eight negations constitute the Middle Way;
because he explains the meaning based on the text, it is called the *Madhyamaka-śāstra-anuvyākhyāna* (Commentary in Accordance with the Middle Way).
The *Madhyamaka-śāstra-anuvyākhyāna* states that the Bodhisattva Nāgārjuna is not the same as Āryadeva.
We should now reconcile this:
because he perfected the supreme path (*jina-mārga*) through the Dragon (*nāga*), he is called Nāgārjuna.
This is because it merely records his name prior to his marriage;
since both monastics and laypeople were mentioned previously,
there is no contradiction in meaning.
Regarding the second section, the explanation of the title of the treatise:
although there are two versions of this treatise, an extensive one and an abridged one,
the abridged version is simply called the *Madhyamaka-śāstra*.
The extensive version adds the element of contemplation (*vipaśyanā*).
However, both these concise and extensive versions possess their own specific significance.
As for what is called "concise":
This refers to principle (*yukti*), teaching (*āgama*), and meaning (*artha*).
"Middle" (*madhya*) is the principle that is explained;
"treatise" (*śāstra*) is the teaching that explains it.
This is not encompassed by principle;
it is not subsumed by non-informative matter (*avijñapti*).
Question: By what means is this so?
Answer: Among the objects signified (*abhidheya*), there are three kinds of middle way:
the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), and that which is neither ultimate nor conventional.
The teaching that signifies these—the discourse—expounds precisely these three.
Therefore, there is nothing that is not gathered by instruction and nothing that is not encompassed by principle.
What is called the "Extensive Original" possesses these three aspects;
it is the path practiced by all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas therein.
"Contemplation" refers to the mind capable of contemplating possessed by all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
When the Buddhas discern through their contemplation and proclaim it with their mouths,
they weigh it as "sūtra."
When a bodhisattva discerns through the mind and articulates it through the mouth,
it is termed a "treatise" (śāstra).
It must possess these three meanings to be complete and perfect.
This has already been explained within the "Mysterious Chapter" (Xuánzhāng).
However, there are three aspects to this:
first, elucidating the "Middle" (zhōng) in contrast to the partiality of the views of annihilationism and eternalism.
This refers to the middle [path] in contrast to the extremes.
Second, regarding the exhaustion of extremes:
the designation "middle" is established with the intent of exhausting the diseases of the extremes.
Therefore, it is called "exhausting the partial within the middle.
Furthermore, from another perspective, the exhaustion of the disease of partiality itself constitutes the middle.
Question: What is the difference between these three: exhausting the partial by means of the partial, the partial as a counterpoint to the partial, and the absolute middle?
The profound intent has already been clarified;
now I shall briefly restate it once more.
Regarding "exhausting the partial within the middle":
It is because it washes away and severs the extremes of eternalism and nihilism that it is forcibly termed "the Middle.
Although it exhausts all partiality, there remains the Middle.
As the Sūtra says:
Sentient beings give rise to views of two kinds:
first, nihilism (annihilationism), and second, eternalism.
That which is neither impermanent nor annihilated is called the Middle Way.
Regarding those who lean toward partiality:
this is called "the Middle" because it refutes the disease of partiality by means of the principle that is its intended meaning (*abhidheya*).
There are generally two kinds of "the Middle that is free from dependence":
first, as it says in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*,
there is the small nirvāṇa and the great nirvāṇa.
Small nirvana is called "bliss" in contrast to suffering;
great nirvana transcends both this suffering and bliss, and is thus named "great bliss.
This very state of transcendence is itself still a form of relativity.
Second, this absolute nirvana cannot be described in terms of suffering or pleasure;
not knowing how else to praise it,
one forcibly names it "pleasure" and designates it as "Great Pleasure."
This alone is the bliss that is free from all relative dependence;
the meaning of the Middle Way is likewise so.
One must deeply perceive this intent.
Question: What is the difference between "solitary emptiness" (*du kong*) and "the ultimate that transcends all dependencies" (*juedai zhong*)?
Answer: Most people do not grasp the essential meaning of solitary emptiness;
they merely rely on the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*.
The eighteen kinds of emptiness are emptinesses that clarify existence;
they are emptinesses that depend on mutual relativity.
That which is neither empty nor existent, having nothing upon which to rely, is designated as "solitary emptiness."
Now, it is said that "only" (*kevala*) is merely a regional dialect.
Upon examining the meaning of "solitary emptiness" (*kevala-śūnyatā*), this is not the case;
rather, because from the very beginning there has ultimately been nothing at all, and only the *dharmatā* of the true mark exists, it is termed "solitary."
This is precisely the orthodox tradition.
The *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states:
"True Suchness alone remains."
It is also with this same intent.
Question: Why is this alone designated by the name "emptiness" (śūnyatā)?
Answer: Because it is ultimately devoid of all afflictions and conditioned phenomena, it is termed "empty."
The *Mahāsannipāta-sūtra* states:
"Because it is ineffable and because it is without marks, it is called emptiness.
The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* states:
Ultimately, they all return to emptiness;
the meaning is likewise so.
Regarding Master Rui’s explanation of the title, there are three parts.
First, the explanation of the name;
second, the intent behind establishing the name;
third, the benefits.
To name something by its "middle" is to illuminate its reality.
Illumination has two meanings:
first, "illumination" (zhào) is glossed as "to manifest."
Establishing this title within this context reveals the actual principle.
These two [terms] serve as metaphors for the title;
for without a lamp, there would be no means by which objects could be illuminated and discerned.
Since there is no means by which that which is not the Middle can manifest the reality of the principle,
it is called "illumination" (*zhào*).
To designate it as a "treatise" (*lùn*) is to exhaust its verbal expression.
"Exhaustion" (jin) is a term signifying thorough completion without remainder. For instance,
in the discourses of the Lesser Vehicle that involve the apprehension of something attained,
the refutation of the heterodox is not exhaustive and the exposition of the orthodox is insufficient.
This is because it is a teaching that leaves something remaining; therefore, it is not called "exhaustive" (*kṣaya*).
That which is contrary to this is designated as "exhaustive.
This is because when the principles of the argument are fully exhausted, the words themselves come to an end.
Therefore, it is said that "all words are exhausted," rather than saying that "wordlessness exhausts [the meaning].
Master Rui merely explained the *Madhyamaka-śāstra* without clarifying the contemplation (*vipaśyanā*).
Because this Middle Way is the principle, it is called "teaching.
Since these two already encompass [the other two], the "contemplation" is not explained separately.
In reality, one does not awaken through names alone; this concludes the second section, which establishes the intent behind the names.
However, the ultimate Way is neither "middle" nor "not middle," and neither "name" nor "not name. Yet,
although in principle it is neither middle nor not middle,
the name "middle" is established by force in order to enable sentient beings to attain awakening.
Regarding the statement that "words cannot be fully exhausted without explanation, and thus one employs provisional discourse to clarify them":
if one does not employ provisional questions and answers to explain these words,
there would be no means by which the words proclaiming the Way could be fully exhausted.
By employing provisional questions and answers to explain these words,
the teachings of the Way are finally made clear.
One may examine this in detail through this text.
Thus we know that it is not the case that there is no speech while one exhaustively weighs all speech.
However, speech is merely discourse (*lun*).

It is simply because one causes [the meaning] to be explained through elegant and alternating expositions that it is said that "speech does not exhaust [the meaning]"; it is by means of discourse that one makes it clear.
In fact, having already explained [the first two],
the third establishes the benefits of the names;
the first clarifies the principles and the teachings.
Next, the benefits obtained are described.
"The reality having been proclaimed" means that the principle has been made manifest;
"the words having been clarified" means that the teaching has been made clear.
The benefits obtained are explained below under the illumination of the bodhisattva’s path and site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*).
Because words are clarified by means of principle,
one awakens to the principle through the teaching.
Thus, the establishment of cause and fruit is achieved.
Furthermore, this *Lotus Sūtra* reveals only the single principle and teaches only the single person.
For those who understand this with clear and far-reaching insight:
I borrow the words of Zhuang Zhou to clarify the meaning of the establishment of cause and effect:
"Abiding in the season and dwelling in accordance with the natural order,
neither sorrow nor joy can enter."
This refers to the Emperor’s "suspended liberation.
This can be explained through two meanings.
First, it signifies that the Bodhisattva, by means of the causal ground of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa), brings forth illumination and manifestation.
Thus, one is forever free from the joy and sorrow of birth and death,
such that neither grief nor pleasure can enter.
Second, that which is bound is called "manifest."
"Non-binding" refers to liberation.
"Binding" refers to being bound by the scales of the extremes of annihilationism and eternalism;
since all views have been stilled, it is termed "liberation."
Now, as for the statement that "obstructions and delusions arise from inverted views," this is the third section,
which sets forth the occasion for composing the treatise.
It is divided into two parts according to the text.
First, the introductory narrative of the origins;
second, the clarification of how Nāgārjuna appeared in the world to shatter delusions and compose this treatise.
The first section consists of two sentences.
First, the delusion of ordinary beings; second, the failure of the sages.
"Delusion of ordinary beings" refers to the ninety-six types of heterodox arts and those who give rise to craving.
"Failure of the sages" refers to those who cling to the Hīnayāna and those who perceive attainment within the Mahāyāna.
These two cases do not fail to be subsumed;
the first refers to the fault of establishing one's own [position],
while the second refers to confusion regarding the received teachings.
In general, delusion consists of two aspects:
first, the cause of delusion;
second, the fruit obtained through delusion.
The two phrases concerning the causes of delusion apply equally to the results. Indeed,
those who remain stagnant in their delusions—
"Stagnation" (zhì) refers to being stuck or attached;
it is the flow that arises from craving.
"Delusion" (huò) refers to being confused.
They are those who give rise to views.
Sentient beings in the cycle of birth and death give rise to attachment while at home and give rise to views when they leave the home life;
thus, they are like the venomous insects and evil spirits of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*.
Within the burning house there are only these two things;
likewise, the roots of birth and death are only craving and views,
as stated in the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*.
Regarding those born with inverted views:
the preceding section clarified the culmination of craving and views;
this sentence next investigates their root.
Thus, those who possess craving and views all arise from inverted and arbitrary perceptions.
As stated in the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*:
Good and evil arise from the body;
the body arises from craving;
and craving arises from the false discrimination of conceptualization.
False conceptualization arises from inversion;
thus, that which is seen through inversion constitutes the root of craving and views for both the laity and those who have left the household life.
Furthermore, since the preceding sentence has already clarified the existence of craving and views:
The latter phrase also contains both inversion and view.
"Inversion" refers to being topsy-turvy;
"view" refers to false conceptualization.
Therefore, in its final manifestation there are not two,
nor are there two in its fundamental essence.
It is by means of this that beings in the three realms are submerged and drowned.
This second section further clarifies the loss of the fruit.
Through the two causes of craving and views, one experiences the two fruits of being submerged and drowning within the three realms.
To be submerged in water is what is meant by "drowning."
When the earth collapses, it becomes a whirlpool.
The Lotus Sūtra says:
"In this way, sentient beings suffering from all these various kinds of pain are submerged within it."
Suffering is likened to a great ocean;
thus, to be submerged within suffering is the meaning of "drowning.
The collapse of the impermanent house of the three realms is the meaning of "falling into ruin."
Thus, the two causes of craving and false views produce the two effects of impermanence and suffering.
As the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* states:
"The two causes of evil spirits and venomous insects produce the two effects of the collapse of the house and the outbreak of fire that burns the dwelling."
Master Rui’s view is entirely consistent with the intent of the *Lotus Sūtra* and the teachings of the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa*.
The partial awakening that arises from those who harbor aversion toward wisdom is the second point,
which distinguishes the errors of the sages.
Since the transgressions of ordinary beings are grave, they are clarified first;
since the transgressions of the noble ones are light, they are distinguished later.
Thus, there is a sequence according to gravity and lightness.
Furthermore, what preceded was the delusion of the external;
now the internal afflictions are being distinguished.
This sequence is also established because the external is heavy while the internal is light.
Regarding the text, there are two parts:
first, the formal exposition of the faults;
second, the mutual elucidation of gains and losses.
The first two lines of the beginning consist of:
first, distinguishing the cause of failure;
second, clarifying the result of failure.
There are two causes for loss,
and there are likewise two results of loss;
these correspond to the aforementioned [causes and results].
Regarding "partial awakening" (*piānwù*):
it is called "awakening" (*wù*) by the sages in contrast to the delusion of ordinary beings;
however, when viewed from the perspective of the Mahāyāna, it is designated as "partial."
Therefore, it is said that they possess partial awakening.
The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states:
"Those of the two vehicles are called persons of crooked view."
Furthermore, it says:
"If one speaks of the absence of giving with the mindset of a śrāvaka or pratyekabuddha,
this is called breaking the precepts and holding wrong views."
The Lotus Sūtra states that those seated there have "squinting eyes.
Having squinting eyes means that what they see is not upright;
that is to say, both the views of emptiness and existence are equally non-upright views.
"It is said that the Buddha was truly born in the royal palace and truly attained parinirvāṇa in the twin śāla groves;
this indicates that what is perceived is not correct.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
The emptiness of the two vehicles is called "mere emptiness" (butong).
Therefore, their view of emptiness is not correct.
Furthermore, the two vehicles lack the Middle Way and right contemplation.
As stated in the Nirvāṇa Sūtra:
"Because one perceives only emptiness and does not perceive non-emptiness,
one does not practice the Middle Way and fails to see the Buddha-nature."
This is called partial awakening.
That which arises from the wisdom of revulsion is the second phrase,
which seeks the root of awakening.
The reason why those of the Two Vehicles attain a partial awakening is that they loathe birth-and-death and long for nirvana,
as the Lotus Sutra says:
First one takes the payment and then removes the filth;
likewise, those of the Two Vehicles, fearing old age, sickness, and death,
sever greed, hatred, and delusion in order to seek nirvana as eternal extinction.
Therefore, it is called "knowledge of revulsion.
As for those who become estranged because of their rigid integrity,
this second section clarifies the attainment of the fruit.
This also consists of two phrases:
the first describes their deluded attachments,
and the second clarifies the attainment of the fruit.
Regarding the term "耿介" (upright and resolute),
